title: Maintaining occupational health, safety and general housekeeping

lessons.title: Health and safety duties on the farm
lessons.html:
The law and your role

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 (OHS Act) applies to farms, packhouses and processing sheds. It places a duty on the employer to provide and maintain, as far as reasonably practicable, a working environment that is safe and without risk to the health of workers. Workers also have duties: to take reasonable care of their own health and safety and that of others, to follow safety rules and instructions, to use the protective equipment provided, and to report unsafe conditions and incidents.

At supervisor level you are the link between the rules and the people doing the work. You make sure the team knows the hazards, follows safe work procedures and reports problems early.

Hazard and risk

  • A hazard is anything that can cause harm: a moving PTO shaft, a chemical, a bull in a crush, a wet floor, an open electrical box.
  • Risk is how likely it is that the hazard will cause harm, and how bad the harm would be.

Common farm hazards

AreaExamples
MachineryTractors rolling over, PTO shafts, augers, chippers, unguarded belts
ChemicalsPesticides, herbicides, fuel, dip, cleaning chemicals
AnimalsKicks, crushing in kraals and crushes, zoonotic diseases
EnvironmentHeat, lightning, snakes, bees, dams
BuildingsSlippery floors, poor lighting, falls from height, electrical faults

Controlling hazards

Work from the most effective control to the least:

  1. Remove the hazard if possible.
  2. Replace it with something safer, such as a less toxic product.
  3. Guard or isolate it, for example PTO guards and locked chemical stores.
  4. Use safe work procedures, training, signs and supervision.
  5. Use personal protective equipment (PPE) as the last line of defence.

Before a task, do a quick check with the team: what can go wrong, and what will we do to prevent it?

lessons.title: Housekeeping, inspections and incident reporting
lessons.html:
Good housekeeping

Housekeeping means keeping the workplace clean, tidy and orderly. Poor housekeeping causes many injuries: people trip over hoses, slip on spilt oil, or are cut by tools left lying around. Untidy stores also attract rats and snakes and make fires more likely.

Housekeeping standards

  • Walkways and emergency exits kept clear at all times.
  • Tools returned to their place after use, sharp edges covered.
  • Spills of oil, fuel or chemicals cleaned up at once using the right absorbent, and the waste disposed of as the farm's procedure says.
  • Chemicals stored in their original labelled containers, in a locked, ventilated store away from food and feed.
  • Waste sorted: general waste, recyclables, empty chemical containers and used oil each in their own place.
  • Fire extinguishers in place, visible, unblocked and inspected.
  • Toilets, wash areas and eating areas kept clean.

Workplace inspections

Use a checklist to inspect your area regularly, for example weekly. Check guards on machines, condition of ladders and tools, first aid box contents, PPE condition, fire equipment, chemical store and housekeeping. Record what you find, who must fix it and by when, and follow up.

Incidents and near misses

An incident is any event that caused, or could have caused, injury or damage. A near miss is an incident where no one was hurt, for example a bin falling from a forklift beside a worker. Near misses are warnings; reporting them prevents the next injury.

  1. Make the area safe and give first aid if trained.
  2. Report to your manager immediately.
  3. Do not move anything at a serious incident scene unless needed to save life or prevent further harm.
  4. Record what happened, where, when, who was involved and witnesses.
  5. Take part in the investigation and in putting corrective actions in place.

Serious injuries must be reported by the employer to the Department of Employment and Labour, and injured workers may need a claim under the Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act. Your accurate records support this.

Key points

  • Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, both employer and workers have safety duties.
  • Identify hazards and control them, using PPE as the last line of defence.
  • Keep walkways clear, clean spills and store chemicals correctly.
  • Inspect your area with a checklist and follow up on findings.
  • Report all incidents and near misses immediately and accurately.

quiz.question: Which law is the main occupational health and safety law that applies to farms in South Africa?

options.text: Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993

quiz.question: What is the difference between a hazard and a risk?

options.text: A hazard can cause harm; risk is how likely and how serious that harm is
They mean exactly the same thing
A risk is a type of PPE
A hazard only applies to chemicals

quiz.question: In the order of controls, where does PPE fall?

options.text: It is the first and best control
It is the last line of defence

quiz.question: A bin falls from a forklift next to a worker but nobody is hurt. What is this?

options.text: A near miss that must be reported
A normal part of the job
In original labelled containers in a locked, ventilated store away from food
In cool drink bottles in the kitchen
